blocks.text: A car's gearbox holds dozens of small gears, cams and bushings. Cutting each from solid bar would waste more than half the metal; pressing them from metal powder and baking them in a furnace wastes almost none, and the part comes out of the press already in its final shape. Powder metallurgy (PM) makes millions of such parts a year at a unit cost that machining cannot match.

blocks.markdown: **Powder metallurgy** forms parts from metal powder instead of from molten or solid metal. The standard press-and-sinter route has three main steps. In **blending** the base powder (for example iron, 50 to 150 $\mu$m particles) is mixed with alloying powders such as graphite or copper and a small amount (about 0.5 to 1 percent by weight, typical) of a lubricant such as zinc stearate, so that every batch has uniform composition and flows into the die. In **compaction** the powder is pressed in a hard die by upper and lower punches at pressures typically 400 to 800 MPa, forming a **green compact** with the shape of the part, strong enough to handle but fragile. In **sintering** the green part is heated in a protective atmosphere to about 70 to 90 percent of the melting temperature (about 1120 $^\circ$C for iron-based parts, typically) for 20 to 45 minutes. The particles bond by atomic diffusion at their contacts, and the compact gains strength without melting.

blocks.title: Porosity and density
blocks.text: Sintered parts contain voids. The **porosity** $P$ is the fraction of the volume that is void, $P=1-\rho/\rho_{th}$, where $\rho$ is the density of the compact (g/cm$^3$) and $\rho_{th}$ is the theoretical density of the solid metal (for iron about 7.87 g/cm$^3$). Equivalently, the density of a sintered part is $\rho=\rho_{th}(1-P)$.

blocks.caption: Density, porosity and mass of a sintered part ($V$ the volume of the part)

blocks.title: Density and mass of a sintered iron part
blocks.prompt: A sintered iron bushing has a porosity of 15 percent and a volume of 12 cm$^3$. Take $\rho_{th}=7.87$ g/cm$^3$. Find its density and mass.
blocks.answer: The density is 6.69 g/cm^3 and the mass is about 80 g.

blocks.markdown: The porosity matters because strength, ductility and stiffness fall as the voids grow, since voids reduce the load-carrying area and concentrate stress. A typical press-and-sinter iron part has 10 to 20 percent porosity and mechanical properties well below wrought iron of the same composition. Porosity is useful in one case: interconnected pores can be impregnated with oil to make self-lubricating bearings, or kept open to make filters. Higher density can be obtained by higher compaction pressure, repressing (sizing or coining) or infiltrating the pores with a lower-melting metal such as copper.

blocks.title: Compaction force
blocks.prompt: A circular flange part has an outside diameter of 60 mm and a pressing area of 1500 mm$^2$ in the die plane. The powder needs a compaction pressure of 600 MPa. Find the press force and the equivalent capacity in tonnes-force (1 tonne-force = 9.81 kN).

steps.text: Force = pressure times pressed area (projected on the punch).

blocks.answer: The press force is 900 kN, about 92 tonnes-force, so the press needs more than this capacity, with margin.

blocks.markdown: Where does PM win over machining? Its strengths are near-net shape with almost no waste, good dimensional repeatability, and a unit cost dominated by powder rather than by long machining time. Its weaknesses are the hard-tooling cost, the limit on part size set by press force (the pressed area times pressure), the limit on shape in the pressing direction (no undercuts or cross holes without machining) and lower strength because of porosity. It is therefore best for **small to medium parts of moderately complex shape made in large volumes**, such as gears, cams, sprockets, bushings and filters.

blocks.title: When PM beats machining
blocks.text: Choose PM when the part is small, the shape can be pressed along one axis, the volume is high enough to recover the die cost (typically tens of thousands of parts), and the loads are moderate. For example, a part of 0.18 kg machined from a 0.42 kg bar wastes 57 percent of the material as swarf, whereas PM uses about 97 percent of the powder.

blocks.title: Design limits
blocks.text: Do not specify thin sections with large height-to-thickness ratios, sharp internal corners, cross holes or undercuts in the pressing direction. Check that the density is uniform: long parts pressed from one side have lower density far from the moving punch.

points: PM sequence: blend powders and lubricant, compact in a die (400 to 800 MPa typical), then sinter below the melting point so particles bond by diffusion.
Density of a sintered part is $\rho=\rho_{th}(1-P)$ and mass $m=\rho V$; strength falls as porosity rises.
Compaction force is pressure times pressed area.
PM is most economical for small, pressable shapes in high volume, since it wastes little material and avoids machining.

questions.stem: What is the correct order of the main steps in press-and-sinter powder metallurgy?

distractorRationale.a: Sintering needs a compact already pressed to shape, so it cannot come first.
distractorRationale.c: The powders must be blended before they can be pressed to a uniform composition.
distractorRationale.d: The green part must be pressed to shape before it can be sintered.

questions.explanation: The powders and lubricant are blended first, pressed to the shape of the part in a die, and the green compact is then heated in a sintering furnace. Reversing any pair of steps is impossible because each needs the output of the previous one.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of sintering a powder compact?

options.text: To melt the powder completely so it flows into the mould
To shape the part to its final dimensions
To bond the particles by diffusion at a temperature below the melting point

questions.correctOptionText: To bond the particles by diffusion at a temperature below the melting point

distractorRationale.a: Sintering is below the melting temperature; complete melting would destroy the shape.
distractorRationale.b: Shape is given by the compaction step, not by sintering.
distractorRationale.c: Sintering reduces but never completely removes porosity.

questions.explanation: At sintering temperature, typically 70 to 90 percent of the melting temperature, atoms diffuse across the particle contacts and form necks, giving the compact strength. The part keeps its shape because it never melts.

questions.stem: A copper sintered part has a porosity of 12 percent. Take the theoretical density of copper as 8.96 g/cm$^3$. Calculate the density of the part in g/cm$^3$.
questions.explanation: Using $\rho=\rho_{th}(1-P)=8.96\times(1-0.12)=7.885$ g/cm$^3$. The void fraction reduces the density in direct proportion.

questions.stem: A sintered iron-based part has a measured density of 6.9 g/cm$^3$. Taking the theoretical density as 7.85 g/cm$^3$, calculate the porosity as a percentage.
questions.explanation: The porosity is $P=1-\rho/\rho_{th}=1-6.9/7.85=0.1210$, i.e. 12.1 percent. A value of this size is typical for press-and-sinter parts.

questions.stem: A sintered steel part has 10 percent porosity and the theoretical density of the steel is 7.85 g/cm$^3$. What is the density of the part?

distractorRationale.b: This subtracts the porosity fraction (0.10) as if it were a density, rather than multiplying by $(1-P)$.
distractorRationale.c: This divides by $(1-P)$ instead of multiplying, giving a density above the theoretical value, which is impossible.
distractorRationale.d: This multiplies by $(1+P)$, again giving a density above the theoretical value.

questions.explanation: The density is $\rho=\rho_{th}(1-P)=7.85\times0.90=7.065$ g/cm$^3$. Porosity can only reduce the density below the theoretical value.

questions.stem: Why is a lubricant such as zinc stearate blended with the metal powder before compaction?

options.text: It raises the porosity of the final part on purpose
It reduces friction between the powder and the die wall and eases ejection of the compact
It makes the powder particles melt together

questions.correctOptionText: It reduces friction between the powder and the die wall and eases ejection of the compact

distractorRationale.a: The lubricant does not alter the sintering temperature and is burnt off at the start of sintering.
distractorRationale.b: Porosity is not increased deliberately; the lubricant is removed before sintering.
distractorRationale.d: Melting does not occur; the lubricant helps pressing, not melting.

questions.explanation: Friction at the die wall causes density gradients and high ejection forces that damage the green part. A small percentage of lubricant lowers the friction and is burned off in the early part of sintering.

questions.stem: A bushing is pressed in the form of a ring with an outside diameter of 40 mm and a centre hole of 10 mm diameter. Calculate the compaction force in kN at a pressure of 550 MPa on the annular pressed area.
questions.explanation: The annular area is $\pi(40^2-10^2)/4=1178.1$ mm$^2$. The force is $F=550\times1178.1=647953$ N, i.e. 648 kN.

questions.stem: Which of the following parts is the best candidate for powder metallurgy rather than machining from bar?

options.text: A single 2 m long drive shaft
A thin-walled hollow part with a cross hole and undercut
A small steel gear needed at 500 000 per year

questions.correctOptionText: A small steel gear needed at 500 000 per year

distractorRationale.a: Long parts cannot be pressed in a die, and one piece cannot recover the tooling cost.
distractorRationale.b: Five prototypes cannot justify the die cost.
distractorRationale.c: Cross holes and undercuts cannot be formed by pressing along one axis.

questions.explanation: A small gear can be pressed to net shape along one axis, high volume repays the die, and PM avoids machining the teeth from bar with a large amount of waste. The other parts fail on size, volume or shape.

questions.stem: Describe the three main stages of the press-and-sinter process and state the purpose of each. Include typical conditions.
markingGuide: Blending: mix base powder, alloy additions and lubricant (about 0.5 to 1 wt%) for uniform composition and easy pressing
Compaction: press in hard die at about 400 to 800 MPa to give the green shape
Green compact is handleable but weak; density non-uniform if long
Sintering: heat at roughly 70 to 90 percent of melting temperature (about 1120 $^\circ$C for iron) in protective atmosphere
Bonding by diffusion; the part does not melt; secondary operations such as sizing may follow
questions.explanation: Blending prepares a uniform, flowable mix, compaction gives the shape and green strength, and sintering develops strength by diffusion bonding below the melting point. Secondary operations such as sizing or impregnation then refine accuracy or properties.

questions.stem: A manufacturer produces 200 000 small iron gears a year by machining from bar, wasting 57 percent of the bar as swarf. Explain why powder metallurgy might be more economical, estimating the effect of porosity on mass and strength, and state two reasons PM might not be suitable.
markingGuide: PM uses about 97 percent of the material versus about 43 percent for machining
Near-net-shape: little or no machining, lower labour and overhead
Die cost is spread over 200 000 parts a year, so tooling per part is small
Porosity reduces density ($\rho=\rho_{th}(1-P)$) so mass is lower but strength and ductility fall
Not suitable if high strength or fatigue are needed, or the shape has undercuts or cross holes, or the volume is too low or the part too large for the press
questions.explanation: PM saves material and machining time and spreads its die cost over a large volume. Its drawbacks are the lower strength caused by porosity and restrictions on size and shape.
